title: The Semmelweis Reflex
author: Mike Fisher
summary: Fisher uses the Vienna maternity wards of the 1840s to isolate a specific and nastier cousin of confirmation bias. Semmelweis found that doctors moving from autopsies to deliveries were killing mothers at three times the midwives' rate, cut mortality from eighteen percent to just above one percent with chlorinated lime, and was rewarded with the loss of his post, ridicule, and death in an asylum at forty seven. Fisher is careful to grant that intelligent people had real grounds to hesitate, since germ theory did not yet exist and the evidence was observational, but insists the deeper obstacle was that accepting the finding meant accepting what it said about the men reading it. He extends the pattern through Halsted's radical mastectomy and Barry Marshall swallowing a culture of Helicobacter pylori, then moves it into the boardroom, where a churn analysis implicating an executive's strategy suddenly becomes a conversation about whether the analysis can be trusted. The remedies are habits rather than cures: separate discomfort from data, state a falsifying condition before the data arrives, protect the messenger in public, and steelman the case against yourself.
points: Fisher distinguishes the reflex from ordinary confirmation bias by the presence of self-implication, which is what makes the evidence intolerable.
He notes the reflex is invisible from the inside because the reaching for objections feels like rigour, so self-interrogation will not catch it.
The business examples are recognisable and specific, from questioned survey sample sizes to postmortems concluding the strategy was right but the execution unlucky.
He ties the piece to his earlier Challenge Network argument, calling the reflex the exam that a network of critics exists to help a leader pass.
The strongest prescription is to name in advance, out loud, the result that would change your mind, before your ego is committed to an answer.
quotes: In the 1840s the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics, and pregnant women in the city knew which one to fear. Doctors and medical students staffed the First Clinic . Midwives ran the Second.

Semmelweis concluded that his colleagues were carrying something invisible from the dead to the living, called it cadaverous particles, and ordered his staff to scrub with chlorinated lime before examining a patient.
Accepting his explanation meant confronting the possibility that for years they had carried death to the patients they were trying to save, on their own hands, and the evidence implicated them.

Ordinary disagreement asks you to revise your picture of the world, and you can usually manage that. Evidence that your own past decisions caused the harm you set out to prevent asks for something else, and you will find yourself reaching for reasons to doubt it.

The more authority you carry, and the more of your identity rides on the practice under review, the further you will reach. From the inside the reaching feels like rigor. You will not catch it by asking yourself whether you are being rigorous.
Nobody in those rooms says out loud that the finding makes them look bad. They ask reasonable questions instead, and request a little more data before anyone acts.
Decide what would change your mind before the data arrives. Say it out loud, in the meeting, while your ego is still uncommitted.
Everyone in the room prices the next piece of bad news by what you do to the person carrying this one. Thank them, promote them, and let the room see you do it.
